items.title: react-native-minimal-webview
items.text:
A React Native WebView that hands you the iOS and Android WebView APIs, instead of wrapping each one in a prop.

It runs on iOS and Android as an Expo module.

API reference · Examples · Native hooks · Migrating from react-native-webview · Extensions · MIT license

items.title: Why it exists
items.text:
react-native-webview wraps each platform API in a prop of its own. When one isn't wrapped, you wait for an upstream PR, or patch or fork the package, even if the change is one platform call.

This package passes the platform APIs through instead:

  • ios and android props: any setting, by its platform name.
  • The ref's get and call: properties and methods, by name.
  • Native hooks: the WKWebView or WebView itself, in your own Swift or Kotlin module.
import { useRef } from 'react';
import { Button, Platform } from 'react-native';
import { WebView, type WebViewRef } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

export function Browser() {
  const ref = useRef<WebViewRef>(null);
  const pageDown = () => {
    if (Platform.OS === 'android') ref.current?.call('webView.pageDown', [true]);
  };
  return (
    <>
      <Button title="Page down" onPress={pageDown} />
      <WebView
        ref={ref}
        source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }}
        style={{ flex: 1 }}
        ios={{ scrollView: { bounces: false } }}
        android={{ settings: { textZoom: 120 } }}
      />
    </>
  );
}

A setting or method a newer SDK adds works without a release of this package: see ios, android and call.

items.title: What it changes from react-native-webview
items.text:
The core adds only what the platform APIs lack:

react-native-webview react-native-minimal-webview Navigation decisions onShouldStartLoadWithRequest, a JS round trip each navigationRules, matched natively Page messaging postMessage strings, any page Typed promise bridge, allowedOrigins only Navigation state onNavigationStateChange events you keep in state useWebViewState(ref) Page camera and microphone Granted to any page on Android, after asking the OS Your app answers onPermissionRequest

The migration guide covers each react-native-webview prop that works differently here.

items.title: When to use something else
items.text:
• Old architecture, Windows or macOS: react-native-webview supports them, this package doesn't. Neither runs on web.
  • Expo Go: the package has native code, so it needs a development build.

items.title: Install
items.text:
npx expo install react-native-minimal-webview

Then rebuild the app (npx expo run:ios, npx expo run:android).

A bare React Native app adds Expo modules first, then installs with its package manager:

npx install-expo-modules@latest
npm install react-native-minimal-webview   # or: yarn add, pnpm add
npx pod-install

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Platform Minimum iOS 17.0: ios.deploymentTarget: '17.0', for example with expo-build-properties Android API 29: android.minSdkVersion: 29, for example with expo-build-properties Expo SDK 53 (React Native 0.79, React 19) Architecture New architecture only

Some features need a newer Android System WebView: which ones.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
import { WebView } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

export function Browser() {
  return <WebView source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }} style={{ flex: 1 }} />;
}

Then pick what you need:

To See Show the URL, progress or a back button Navigation state Keep the WebView on your sites, open the rest externally Navigation rules Call the page from the app, and the app from the page The bridge Change a WebView setting Platform settings Share cookies with native requests Cookies Run a script on every page Scripts Load bundled HTML Local files Answer file pickers, permissions and downloads Page requests Use the native WKWebView or WebView Native hooks Bring back basicAuthCredential, onScroll and other react-native-webview props @react-native-minimal-webview/extensions

items.title: Contributing
items.text: CONTRIBUTING.md has the setup, the checks and the on-device suites.

items.title: Android System WebView versions
items.text:
Some features need a newer Android System WebView than the minimum Android version brings. This page says why the version matters, how to check and update a device's, and how to test the old ones. Each item's API reference gives the version it needs.

Android System WebView updates apart from Android, so a device's API level doesn't tell you its WebView.

The core checks each feature at run time. On an older WebView the feature is off, and nothing crashes.

items.title: What needs a newer WebView
items.text:
• evaluate
  • blob: downloads with onDownload
  • The bridge
  • injectedScripts
  • pendingUrl
  • onLoadStart and onLoadEnd for a load that never commits
  • SSL errors on back and forward loads in onError
  • backForwardCacheEnabled on by default

A WebSettingsCompat or WebViewCompat key, a compat method through get or call, and WebView.android.preconnect depend on an androidx.webkit feature instead of a WebView version. The keys' and preconnect's TSDoc name it.

items.title: Check a device's WebView
items.text:
The version is the Chrome version in the WebView's user agent: read WebView.android.defaultUserAgent and look for Chrome/<version>.

On a connected device, adb shell dumpsys webviewupdate names the WebView package in use and its version.

items.title: Update a device's WebView
items.text: Update Android System WebView in the Play Store. On an emulator, use a Google APIs system image: a Play Store image updates WebView in the background, so its version moves under your tests.

items.title: Test the oldest versions
items.text: An emulator with a Google APIs image keeps the WebView its image shipped with, and the images of older API levels ship older WebViews. Run the app there to see the features above off. CONTRIBUTING lists the images for the oldest supported versions and how to create the emulators.

items.title: Examples
items.text: Examples of the main interfaces. What each prop, method and type does is in its TSDoc, generated into the API reference.

items.title: Navigation state
items.text:
import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';
import { BackHandler, Button } from 'react-native';
import { WebView, useWebViewState, type WebViewRef } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

export function Browser() {
  const ref = useRef<WebViewRef>(null);
  const { canGoBack } = useWebViewState(ref);

  // Android's back button is the app's to handle
  useEffect(() => {
    const subscription = BackHandler.addEventListener('hardwareBackPress', () => {
      if (!canGoBack) return false;
      ref.current?.goBack();
      return true;
    });
    return () => subscription.remove();
  }, [canGoBack]);

  return (
    <>
      <Button title="Back" disabled={!canGoBack} onPress={() => ref.current?.goBack()} />
      <WebView ref={ref} source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }} style={{ flex: 1 }} />
    </>
  );
}

items.title: Outside React
items.text:
import { WebView, createWebViewRef } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

export const webView = createWebViewRef();

// A push notification handler, say
function onInboxNotification() {
  if (webView.getState().url.startsWith('https://example.com/inbox')) webView.current?.reload();
}

<WebView ref={webView} source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }} style={{ flex: 1 }} />;

items.title: Navigation rules
items.text:
import { WebView, defaultNavigationRules } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

export function Site() {
  return (
    <WebView
      source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }}
      style={{ flex: 1 }}
      navigationRules={[
        { host: ['pay.example.com'], action: 'ask' }, // onNavigationRequest decides
        { host: ['example.com', '*.example.com'], action: 'allow' },
        { scheme: ['http', 'https'], mainFrame: false, action: 'allow' }, // iframes
        { scheme: ['tel', 'mailto'], action: 'external' }, // also from an iframe
        { scheme: ['http', 'https'], action: 'external' }, // other sites, and new windows
        ...defaultNavigationRules, // file: blocked, other schemes external from a user gesture
      ]}
      onNavigationRequest={({ url }) =>
        url.startsWith('https://pay.example.com/checkout') ? 'allow' : 'block'
      }
      onNavigation={({ url, action, rule }) => console.log(action, url, rule)}
    />
  );
}

items.title: The bridge
items.text:
import { useEffect, useMemo } from 'react';
import { Button, Platform, Share } from 'react-native';
import { WebView, createBridge } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

type Methods = {
  share: { params: { url: string }; result: boolean }; // handled in React Native
  getCartCount: { result: number }; // handled by the page
};
type Events = { themeChanged: 'light' | 'dark' };

export function Shop() {
  // Once: a new bridge recreates the WebView
  const bridge = useMemo(
    () => createBridge<Methods, Events>({ allowedOrigins: ['https://example.com'] }),
    []
  );

  // handle returns the unsubscribe, which is the cleanup
  useEffect(
    () =>
      bridge.handle('share', async ({ url }) => {
        const { action } = await Share.share(Platform.OS === 'ios' ? { url } : { message: url });
        return action === Share.sharedAction;
      }),
    [bridge]
  );

  return (
    <>
      <Button title="Dark" onPress={() => bridge.emit('themeChanged', 'dark')} />
      <Button title="Cart" onPress={async () => console.log(await bridge.call('getCartCount'))} />
      <WebView bridge={bridge} source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }} style={{ flex: 1 }} />
    </>
  );
}

items.title: In the page
items.text:
A page on an allowed origin has the same four methods on window.nativeBridge, as Bridge describes.

// A module script
const cart = [];
window.nativeBridge.handle('getCartCount', () => cart.length);
window.nativeBridge.on('themeChanged', (theme) => {
  document.documentElement.dataset.theme = theme;
});

const shared = await window.nativeBridge.call('share', { url: location.href }, { timeoutMs: 0 }); // the share sheet waits on the user

items.title: Platform settings
items.text:
Any setting by its platform name, and any public method through call.

import { AndroidConstants, IOSConstants, WebView } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

<WebView
  source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }}
  style={{ flex: 1 }}
  ios={{
    configuration: { dataDetectorTypes: IOSConstants.DataDetectorTypes.link }, // WKWebViewConfiguration: read once, at creation
    preferences: { minimumFontSize: 12 }, // WKPreferences
    webpagePreferences: { allowsContentJavaScript: false }, // WKWebpagePreferences
    webView: { allowsBackForwardNavigationGestures: true }, // WKWebView
    scrollView: { bounces: false }, // its UIScrollView
  }}
  android={{
    settings: { textZoom: 120, cacheMode: AndroidConstants.WebSettings.LOAD_NO_CACHE }, // WebSettings
    webView: { overScrollMode: 2, acceptThirdPartyCookies: true }, // WebView
  }}
/>;

items.title: Reading and calling
items.text:
The ref of a mounted WebView, here from createWebViewRef (Outside React), has the methods.

import { IOSConstants, createWebViewRef } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

const ref = createWebViewRef(); // pass it as the `<WebView ref={ref}>`

const bounces = await ref.current?.get('scrollView.bounces'); // iOS; 'settings.textZoom' on Android

// Android: a public method of settings, webView, cookieManager or webStorage
await ref.current?.call('webStorage.deleteAllData');
await ref.current?.call('cookieManager.removeAllCookies');

// iOS: an Objective-C selector
await ref.current?.call('websiteDataStore.removeDataOfTypes:modifiedSince:completionHandler:', [
  { set: [IOSConstants.WebsiteDataType.cookies, IOSConstants.WebsiteDataType.localStorage] },
  { date: 0 },
]);
const png = await ref.current?.call('webView.takeSnapshotWithConfiguration:completionHandler:', [
  null,
]); // base64

items.title: Cookies
items.text:
Cookies go through call, as in Reading and calling.

import { createWebViewRef } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

const ref = createWebViewRef(); // pass it as the `<WebView ref={ref}>`
const token = 'SESSION_TOKEN'; // your session's value

// iOS: the WebView's data store (`sharedCookies` syncs it with the app's)
await ref.current?.call('httpCookieStore.setCookie:completionHandler:', [
  { cookie: { Name: 'session', Value: token, Domain: 'example.com', Path: '/', Secure: 'TRUE' } },
]);
const cookies = await ref.current?.call('httpCookieStore.getAllCookies:'); // [{ Name, Value, Domain, Path, … }]

// Android: the app-wide CookieManager
await ref.current?.call('cookieManager.setCookie', [
  'https://example.com',
  `session=${token}; Secure`,
]);
const header = await ref.current?.call('cookieManager.getCookie', ['https://example.com']); // 'session=…; other=…'

items.title: Before the first page
items.text: The calls need a mounted WebView. Mount it with { uri: 'about:blank' }, and set the real source once the cookie is set.

items.title: Scripts
items.text:
import { WebView, createWebViewRef } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

const ref = createWebViewRef();
const config = { apiUrl: 'https://api.example.com' };

<WebView
  ref={ref}
  source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }}
  style={{ flex: 1 }}
  injectedScripts={[
    { code: `window.config = ${JSON.stringify(config)}`, origins: ['https://example.com'] },
  ]}
/>;

const title = await ref.current?.evaluate('document.title'); // an expression, not statements
await ref.current?.evaluate(`(() => { document.body.style.background = 'red'; })()`);

items.title: Local files
items.text:
A bundled file loads from its file:// URI, such as expo-asset's localUri. WebViewSource has each platform's file access.

import { useAssets } from 'expo-asset';
import { WebView } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

export function LocalPages() {
  const [assets] = useAssets(require('./page.html'));
  return (
    <>
      <WebView
        source={{ html: '<img src="logo.png">', baseUrl: 'https://example.com' }}
        style={{ flex: 1 }}
      />
      {assets?.[0]?.localUri && (
        <WebView
          source={{ uri: assets[0].localUri }}
          style={{ flex: 1 }}
          android={{ settings: { allowFileAccess: true } }}
        />
      )}
    </>
  );
}

items.title: File inputs
items.text:
import * as DocumentPicker from 'expo-document-picker';
import * as ImagePicker from 'expo-image-picker';
import { WebView } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

<WebView
  source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }}
  style={{ flex: 1 }}
  onFileRequest={async ({ accept, multiple, capture }) => {
    if (capture) {
      const photo = await ImagePicker.launchCameraAsync();
      return photo.canceled ? null : photo.assets.map((asset) => asset.uri);
    }
    const mimeTypes = accept.filter((type) => type.includes('/'));
    const result = await DocumentPicker.getDocumentAsync({
      type: mimeTypes.length ? mimeTypes : '*/*',
      multiple,
    });
    return result.canceled ? null : result.assets.map((asset) => asset.uri);
  }}
/>;

items.title: Permissions
items.text:
import { Camera } from 'expo-camera';
import { WebView } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

<WebView
  source={{ uri: 'https://meet.example.com' }}
  style={{ flex: 1 }}
  onPermissionRequest={async ({ origin, resources }) => {
    if (origin !== 'https://meet.example.com') return false;
    if (resources.some((resource) => resource !== 'camera')) return false;
    return (await Camera.requestCameraPermissionsAsync()).granted;
  }}
/>;

items.title: Fullscreen video
items.text:
On Android, this lets a portrait-locked app rotate while a video is fullscreen.

import * as ScreenOrientation from 'expo-screen-orientation';
import { WebView } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

<WebView
  source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }}
  style={{ flex: 1 }}
  onFullscreenChange={({ active }) =>
    active
      ? ScreenOrientation.unlockAsync()
      : ScreenOrientation.lockAsync(ScreenOrientation.OrientationLock.PORTRAIT_UP)
  }
/>;

items.title: Downloads
items.text:
preview() needs expo-file-system 58 or later.

import { File } from 'expo-file-system';
import { WebView } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

<WebView
  source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }}
  style={{ flex: 1 }}
  onDownload={(result) =>
    result.ok ? new File(result.uri).preview() : console.warn('download failed', result.kind)
  }
/>;

items.title: Native hooks
items.text: The native hooks guide builds one, from module to the extensions prop.

items.title: Migrating from react-native-webview
items.text:
This page maps each react-native-webview prop to its counterpart here, and lists the defaults and behavior that differ and recipes for what has no prop. The requirements are in the README.

Most props are platform settings by the same name: bounces is ios={{ scrollView: { bounces: false } }}, and textZoom is android={{ settings: { textZoom: 120 } }}. Android keys are setter names without set, so setBuiltInZoomControls is android.settings.builtInZoomControls.

The keys autocomplete, and an enum string becomes a constant: cacheMode: 'LOAD_NO_CACHE' is AndroidConstants.WebSettings.LOAD_NO_CACHE (platform settings).

items.title: Props with no counterpart
items.text: react-native-webview Why autoManageStatusBarEnabled iOS shows WebKit's own fullscreen useSharedProcessPool WKProcessPool has had no effect since iOS 15 ignoreSilentHardwareSwitch react-native-webview keeps a silent <audio> playing in the page for it enableApplePay Apple Pay works with injected scripts since iOS 16 lackPermissionToDownloadMessage A download lands in the app's cache, which needs no permission

items.title: What else changes
items.text:
onNavigationStateChange keeps its name, but fires on every state change, progress and title included. onLoadStart and onLoadEnd keep theirs too, and get the NavigationState instead of a native event. userAgent is the same prop.

Remove the LSApplicationQueriesSchemes (iOS) and <queries> (Android) entries you added for the schemes a page opens (onOpenExternal).

items.title: onShouldStartLoadWithRequest
items.text:
Navigation rules replace the callback, and the first rule that matches decides.

import { WebView } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

// Stands in for what your onShouldStartLoadWithRequest callback decided
const isTrusted = (url: string) => url.startsWith('https://example.com/');

export function Browser() {
  return (
    <WebView
      source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }}
      navigationRules={[
        { host: ['example.com'], action: 'allow' },
        { scheme: ['http', 'https'], mainFrame: false, action: 'allow' }, // iframes
        { mainFrame: true, action: 'ask' }, // the rest: onNavigationRequest answers
      ]}
      onNavigationRequest={({ url }) => (isTrusted(url) ? 'allow' : 'block')}
      style={{ flex: 1 }}
    />
  );
}

Your rules replace the defaults, defaultNavigationRules: spread it after yours to keep them.

A rule decides natively, so a busy JS thread doesn't hold a navigation up. react-native-webview's Android blocks the UI thread while it waits for the callback, and lets the navigation through when the callback is late. Its iOS waits for the answer.

The request has mainFrame in place of isTopFrame, and userInitiated in place of navigationType: 'click'. It has no mainDocumentURL. A new window (onOpenWindow) is a request with newWindow: true.

react-native-webview's iOS also asks about the source load, reloads, back/forward and form POSTs. The rules skip them (navigationRules).

After the rules block a server redirect, the state is the page before it, with outcome cancelled. react-native-webview reports the redirecting URL as still loading (iOS), or the blocked URL as loaded (Android).

items.title: injectJavaScript
items.text:
evaluate takes an expression, not statements, and resolves with its value (evaluate).

Wrap the statements you passed injectJavaScript in a function you call, without the trailing true;, as in the scripts example.

items.title: postMessage and onMessage
items.text:
The bridge replaces both, with calls that return promises, and events, in both directions. It serves only the origins you allow.

Pages that use window.ReactNativeWebView.postMessage and message events keep working with reactNativeWebViewMessages in injectedScripts. Its example shows what replaces onMessage and postMessage.

items.title: incognito
items.text:
On iOS, a non-persistent data store keeps the WebView's cookies, cache and storage, and they go with the WebView.

Android has no incognito WebView. react-native-webview's incognito clears the app-wide cookies, the cache, the history and the form data, turns the cache off, and turns password and form-data saving off. This recipe clears the cookies and the cache and turns the cache off before the page loads. A new WebView has no history, WebView doesn't save form data since API 26, and password saving is deprecated.

The first source is blank, as for cookies before the first page:

import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react';
import { Platform } from 'react-native';
import {
  AndroidConstants,
  WebView,
  type WebViewRef,
  type WebViewSource,
} from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

export function PrivateBrowser() {
  const ref = useRef<WebViewRef>(null);
  const [source, setSource] = useState<WebViewSource>({ uri: 'about:blank' });

  useEffect(() => {
    (async () => {
      if (Platform.OS === 'android') {
        await ref.current?.call('cookieManager.removeAllCookies'); // app-wide, as in react-native-webview
        await ref.current?.call('webView.clearCache', [true]);
      }
      setSource({ uri: 'https://example.com' });
    })();
  }, []);

  return (
    <WebView
      ref={ref}
      source={source}
      ios={{ configuration: { websiteDataStore: 'nonPersistent' } }}
      android={{ settings: { cacheMode: AndroidConstants.WebSettings.LOAD_NO_CACHE } }}
      style={{ flex: 1 }}
    />
  );
}

items.title: Loading and error screens
items.text:
Draw the loading and error views yourself, over the WebView, from the navigation state and onError:

import { useRef, useState } from 'react';
import { ActivityIndicator, Button, StyleSheet, Text, View } from 'react-native';
import {
  WebView,
  useWebViewState,
  type LoadErrorEvent,
  type WebViewRef,
} from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

export function Browser() {
  const ref = useRef<WebViewRef>(null);
  const { loading } = useWebViewState(ref);
  const [error, setError] = useState<LoadErrorEvent | null>(null);

  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1 }}>
      <WebView
        ref={ref}
        source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }}
        onError={(e) => e.kind !== 'http' && setError(e)} // on 'http' the site's own error page shows
        onLoadStart={() => setError(null)}
        style={{ flex: 1 }}
      />
      {error ? (
        <View style={[StyleSheet.absoluteFill, { alignItems: 'center', justifyContent: 'center' }]}>
          <Text>Could not load the page</Text>
          <Button title="Retry" onPress={() => ref.current?.reload()} />
        </View>
      ) : loading ? (
        <ActivityIndicator style={StyleSheet.absoluteFill} />
      ) : null}
    </View>
  );
}

items.title: Scroll position
items.text:
An injected script can report the main frame's scroll position over the bridge, at most once per frame. For the offsets during a bounce or a pinch too, use the onScroll extension.

import { useEffect, useMemo, useState } from 'react';
import { Text } from 'react-native';
import { WebView, createBridge, type InjectedScript } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

const scrollScript: InjectedScript = {
  code: `{ // a block: an origins ['*'] script shares the page's global scope
  let queued = false;
  addEventListener('scroll', () => {
    if (queued) return;
    queued = true;
    requestAnimationFrame(() => { queued = false; window.nativeBridge?.emit('scroll', { x: scrollX, y: scrollY }); });
  }, { passive: true });
}`,
  origins: ['*'], // nativeBridge exists only on the bridge's allowedOrigins
};

export function Browser() {
  const bridge = useMemo(() => createBridge({ allowedOrigins: ['https://example.com'] }), []);
  const [scroll, setScroll] = useState({ x: 0, y: 0 });

  useEffect(() => bridge.on('scroll', (position) => setScroll(position as { x: number; y: number })), [bridge]);

  return (
    <>
      <Text>{scroll.y}</Text>
      <WebView
        source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }}
        bridge={bridge}
        injectedScripts={[scrollScript]}
        style={{ flex: 1 }}
      />
    </>
  );
}

items.title: Native hooks
items.text: A native hook is Swift or Kotlin in your own Expo module that gets the real WKWebView or WebView behind a <WebView>. This guide covers when to write one, how to write one, and how it shares the WebView with the core.

items.title: When to write one
items.text:
Reach for a hook when the props and the ref can't do the job:

To Use Change a setting The ios and android props Read a property or call a method once The ref's get and call Bring back a react-native-webview prop An extension, a hook someone already wrote Handle WebView callbacks, keep native state, or subclass the WebView A native hook

A hook can implement any delegate or client callback. It runs natively, with no JS round trip.

items.title: How a hook works
items.text:
1. Your module registers the hook under a key when the app starts.
  2. The app turns the hook on for a WebView by passing its extension in the extensions prop; HookExtension.options says when it is on or off.
  3. The core calls the hook's attach with the native WebView and a context.
  4. The hook adds its delegates or clients to the context, talks to JS through it, and registers its cleanup with context.onDestroyed.

items.title: Write a hook
items.text: This builds a hook that counts page loads, reports each one to JS, and answers ref.hook calls. It is a trimmed sample.pageCounter from sample-extension.

items.title: 1. Create a module
items.text:
npx create-expo-module@latest --local page-counter

This creates modules/page-counter in your app. A hook in a published package works the same way, with react-native-minimal-webview as a peer dependency.

items.title: 2. Depend on the core
items.text:
In ios/PageCounter.podspec, replace the template's s.platforms with the core's iOS 17.0, or importing the core fails to compile, and add the core:

s.platforms = { :ios => '17.0' }
s.dependency 'MinimalWebView'

In the module's android/build.gradle:

dependencies {
  implementation project(':react-native-minimal-webview')
}

items.title: 3. Register the hook on iOS
items.text:
In ios/PageCounterModule.swift:

import ExpoModulesCore
import MinimalWebView
import WebKit

public class PageCounterModule: Module {
  public func definition() -> ModuleDefinition {
    Name("PageCounter")
    OnCreate {
      MinimalWebViewHooks.register("myApp.pageCounter") { _, context in
        let counter = PageCounter(context: context)
        context.navigationDelegates.append(counter)
        context.handle("count") { _, reply in reply(counter.count) }
      }
    }
  }
}

private final class PageCounter: NSObject, WKNavigationDelegate {
  private let context: WebViewContext
  private(set) var count = 0

  init(context: WebViewContext) {
    self.context = context
  }

  func webView(_ webView: WKWebView, didFinish navigation: WKNavigation!) {
    count += 1
    context.emit("pageLoaded", ["count": count])
  }
}

items.title: 4. Register the hook on Android
items.text:
In android/src/main/java/expo/modules/pagecounter/PageCounterModule.kt:

package expo.modules.pagecounter

import android.webkit.WebView
import android.webkit.WebViewClient
import expo.modules.kotlin.modules.Module
import expo.modules.kotlin.modules.ModuleDefinition
import expo.modules.minimalwebview.MinimalWebViewHooks
import expo.modules.minimalwebview.WebViewContext

class PageCounterModule : Module() {
  override fun definition() = ModuleDefinition {
    Name("PageCounter")
    OnCreate {
      MinimalWebViewHooks.register("myApp.pageCounter") { _, context ->
        val counter = PageCounter(context)
        context.clients += counter
        context.handle("count") { _, reply -> reply(counter.count) }
      }
    }
  }
}

private class PageCounter(private val context: WebViewContext) : WebViewClient() {
  var count = 0
    private set

  override fun onPageFinished(view: WebView, url: String?) {
    count += 1
    context.emit("pageLoaded", mapOf("count" to count))
  }
}

items.title: 5. Describe the hook to JS
items.text:
Replace the generated index.ts with a function that returns the hook's HookExtension, and delete the generated src/, ios/PageCounterView.swift and android/.../PageCounterView.kt: they hold the template's view and module wrappers, which nothing uses now.

import type { HookEvent, HookExtension } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

type PageLoaded = HookEvent<'pageLoaded', { count: number }>;

export const pageCounter = (onLoaded: (count: number) => void): HookExtension => ({
  key: 'myApp.pageCounter',
  onEvent: (event) => {
    if (event.name !== 'pageLoaded') return; // relative to the key
    onLoaded((event as PageLoaded).payload.count);
  },
});

items.title: 6. Use it
items.text:
Pass the extension in the WebView's extensions prop:

import { useRef, useState } from 'react';
import { Button } from 'react-native';
import { WebView, type WebViewRef } from 'react-native-minimal-webview';

import { pageCounter } from '../modules/page-counter';

export function Browser() {
  const ref = useRef<WebViewRef>(null);
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  const logCount = async () => {
    console.log(await ref.current?.hook('myApp.pageCounter', 'count')); // the handler's reply
  };
  return (
    <>
      <Button title={`${count} pages`} onPress={logCount} />
      <WebView
        ref={ref}
        source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }}
        style={{ flex: 1 }}
        extensions={[pageCounter(setCount)]}
      />
    </>
  );
}

Then rebuild the app: npx expo run:ios, npx expo run:android.

items.title: Talk to JS
items.text:
Everything crosses as JSON.

Native JS context.emit(name, payload) The extension's onEvent gets <name> context.ask(name, payload, onAnswer) onEvent's return value, a promise awaited, is the answer context.handle(method, handler) ref.hook(key, method, args) resolves with the reply context.options, context.onOptionsChange The extension's options; a change arrives live

When an ask goes unanswered, and how a failing or silent handle handler reaches JS, are on ask and handle in Hooks.swift and Hooks.kt.

items.title: Share the WebView with the core
items.text:
The core keeps the WebView's own delegate and client slots. Your hook adds to the context's lists instead:

A callback the core also handles reaches the core first, then each hook. A decision, such as whether a navigation loads or a page gets the camera, goes to the first hook that implements it, and switches off the props that make it, such as navigationRules. The rules are on navigationDelegates and clients in Hooks.swift and Hooks.kt.

Leave alone what the core owns, listed at the top of those files.

items.title: Lifecycle
items.text:
When What the hook gets A WebView with its key mounts Android: the webViewFactory, if it has one. Then configure, if it has one, then attach The page ends: a navigation commits, a crash, or unmount Its onDocumentEnd handlers run. Reset per-page state there. Its options change Its onOptionsChange handlers run, without a reload Its key turns on after mount attach runs then, unless the hook has configure or its own WebView class Its key is removed, or its options become null or false onOptionsChange with null: the hook is off and stays attached. When it turns on again, onOptionsChange runs with the new options. The renderer crashes iOS: onDocumentEnd with crashed; the WKWebView reloads and nothing attaches again. Android: onDocumentEnd, then onDestroyed, with CRASHED; then the factory, configure and attach run again, on a new context. The WebView unmounts onDocumentEnd, then onDestroyed, with closing: clean up there.

DocumentEnd (Swift, Kotlin) says exactly when a page ends, and what each reason means. onDestroyed says what is still alive when it runs.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Register in OnCreate, under a key prefixed with your package's name: register in Hooks.swift and Hooks.kt has the rules.
  • Use the context as WebViewContext there says: some members work from any thread, the rest from the main thread.

[androidJvm] enum DocumentEnd : Enum<DocumentEnd>

Why a Document ended, as WebViewContext.onDocumentEnd and WebViewContext.onDestroyed report it.

A Document is the main-frame page a WebView shows now: from a navigation's commit, a back-forward-cache restore or a failed load's error page included, to the next commit, a renderer crash or the view closing.

items.title: register
items.text:
[androidJvm] fun register(key: String, webViewFactory: (Context) -> WebView? = null, configure: (WebView, WebViewContext) -> Unit? = null, attach: (WebView, WebViewContext) -> Unit)

Registers the hook for key. Call it from your module's OnCreate, before the first WebView.

The same register call running again replaces its hook: a JS reload creates the modules anew and runs their OnCreate again. A helper that calls register for other code is one call, so a second hook through it replaces the first silently.

The hook attaches to each WebView whose extensions prop has an extension with key that is on; HookExtension.options says when. After a renderer crash it attaches again, to the WebView that replaces the dead one.

Hooks attach in registration order, which across packages is autolinking's (packages sorted by name), so an earlier hook's clients come first. A hook whose key turns on after the WebView was created attaches after the hooks attached already; after a crash it takes its place in registration order again.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
androidJvm

key the key of the app's extension that turns on the hook. Keys are global, so prefix yours with your package's name. core is reserved for the package's own events: a hook under it is logged and not registered. webViewFactory makes each WebView this hook is attached to, on or off: the first one and each after a renderer crash, as a subclass that overrides what WebView lets a subclass override. Null leaves it to the other hooks. When the attached hooks name different factories (the same object is one), the first one's in registration order makes the WebView, and a core.warning names the others. Those still attach, so check the class attach gets. configure runs on the main thread as soon as each WebView this hook is attached to, on or off, is made, before the package sets it up (WebViewCompat.setProfile goes here). It gets the same context that attach gets next for that WebView, so state it makes can be keyed by the context. attach runs on the main thread once the WebView has its settings and is in the view hierarchy, so what it sets wins over those settings. Register what to run when that WebView goes away with WebViewContext.onDestroyed. Document-start scripts you add here run before the package's, so window.nativeBridge and injectedScripts aren't there yet (on iOS yours run after them).

items.title: Throws
items.text: IllegalStateException when a different hook is registered under key already. Don't rely on it: a minified build can't tell the two apart and may replace the first hook instead, so give each hook its own key.

items.title: WebViewContext
items.text:
[androidJvm] interface WebViewContext

One WebView as one hook sees it, for one attach.

Each attach gets a new context, and the handlers registered on it belong to that attach: after a renderer crash, the new WebView's attach registers them again.

Call emit and ask from any thread, and the rest on the main thread, where the handlers and the answers run.

The hook is on while its extension's options are not null or false; HookExtension.options says what off means. onOptionsChange still runs while it is off, so the hook can release what it holds, and again when the hook turns on.

A context kept after its attach ended (the view closed, or a renderer crash replaced the WebView) does nothing: its lists reach no WebView and its emit reaches nothing.

items.title: ask
items.text:
[androidJvm] abstract fun ask(name: String, payload: Map<String, Any?>, onAnswer: (Any?) -> Unit)

Sends the event as emit does, and calls onAnswer with JS's answer: the extension's onEvent return value, a promise awaited. A number answers as a Double.

It answers null when the handler throws or there is none, or when the Document ends first; there is no timeout. It answers null at once while the hook is off, and after the context's attach ended. An ask made before the WebView's first commit (in attach) belongs to the Document that commit opens.

items.title: chromeClients
items.text:
[androidJvm] abstract val chromeClients: MutableList<WebChromeClient>

The hook chrome clients, routed as clients are.

Overriding the deprecated onConsoleMessage(String, Int, String) counts as overriding onConsoleMessage, and overriding onReceivedIcon turns favicon downloads back on.

items.title: clients
items.text:
[androidJvm] abstract val clients: MutableList<WebViewClient>

The hook clients, in order; add yours in attach. While the hook is off, none of them gets a callback.

Each callback reaches the clients by one of these rules:

  • A callback that returns a decision goes to the first client that overrides it, instead of the core and the app's props.
  • Every other callback reaches the core first, then each client that overrides it.

Taking a decision the core makes from the app's props or their defaults switches them off, the default navigation rules' security checks included, and a core.warning names the callback and what stops applying.

A client that overrides shouldOverrideUrlLoading decides navigations instead of the navigation rules, which still decide new windows unless a chrome client overrides onCreateWindow. A new window the rules allow loads in place with loadUrl, which doesn't reach shouldOverrideUrlLoading (on iOS that load reaches the deciding delegate).

A decision more than one client overrides still goes only to the first, and a core.warning names it. Each warning comes once per WebView, when its decision first comes.

Overriding a variant the base class forwards to counts as overriding the callback: WebViewClientCompat's onReceivedError, onSafeBrowsingHit and shouldOverrideUrlLoading(WebView, String), and the platform's deprecated shouldOverrideUrlLoading(WebView, String), shouldInterceptRequest(WebView, String) and 4-argument onReceivedError.

shouldInterceptRequest runs on a background thread.

items.title: emit
items.text:
[androidJvm] abstract fun emit(name: String, payload: Map<String, Any?>)

Sends an event to JS as <key>.<name>: the extension's onEvent gets { name, payload }, with name relative to the key. It is dropped while the hook is off, and after the context's attach ended.

items.title: handle
items.text:
[androidJvm] abstract fun handle(method: String, handler: (args: List<Any?>, reply: (Any?) -> Unit) -> Unit)

Answers JS's ref.hook("<key>", method, args): handler gets the arguments and calls reply exactly once.

The arguments come in JSON types (a number as an Int, Long or Double), and the reply must be a value JSON can encode. One handler per method: the last one wins.

A handler that throws, or a reply JSON can't encode, rejects the JS call with native_error. A handler that never replies leaves the call waiting until the WebView unmounts: a navigation or a crash doesn't settle it.

items.title: onDestroyed
items.text:
[androidJvm] abstract fun onDestroyed(handler: (DocumentEnd) -> Unit)

Runs handler once this attach's WebView is destroyed: with DocumentEnd.CLOSING at unmount, or with DocumentEnd.CRASHED after a renderer crash. It comes after the onDocumentEnd handlers that get the same reason, and the context does nothing by then.

Clean up here, and release what must outlive the WebView, such as a ProfileStore profile.

Runs handler at each end of the Document (see DocumentEnd), after the core's own resets: per-page state belongs here.

Return true to take it: neither of those gets it then. The hooks that are on are offered it in registration order, and the first that takes it ends the round.

The hook turns off when the extension is removed, or its options become null or false. A change from one off value to another doesn't run it.

This hook's extension's options, the new ones after a change; null while the hook is off.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
key

The key of the app’s extension that turns on the hook. Keys are global, so prefix yours with your package’s name.

webViewClass

The WKWebView subclass that each WebView enabling this hook is made from, to override what WKWebView lets a subclass override; nil leaves the class to the other hooks. When the enabled hooks name different classes, the first one’s in registration order makes the view, and a core.warning names the others. Those still attach, so check the class attach gets. The hidden view that window.open('') gets is always a plain WKWebView.

configure

Runs before the WKWebView exists, with the configuration it is created from: after the ios.configuration settings and before the bridge, so replacing the user content controller is fine. User scripts you add stay, and run after the package’s. It gets the same context that attach gets next, so state it makes can be keyed by the context. window.open('') opens a hidden WKWebView from this configuration: your user scripts run in it and your script message handlers get its messages, so compare message.webView with the WKWebView attach gets.

attach

Runs once the WKWebView exists and its settings are applied, so what it sets wins over them. Register what to run when the view goes away with onDestroyed(_:). A web content process crash reloads the same WKWebView, so nothing attaches again (see DocumentEnd.crashed).

file

With line, the call site that tells a reload from a second hook; leave both to their defaults.

line

The call site’s line, with file.

items.title: Discussion
items.text:
Call it from your module’s OnCreate, before the first WebView.

A second hook under a key stops the app with fatalError, naming the key and both call sites. A hook under core is logged and not registered.

The same call running again replaces its hook: a JS reload creates the modules anew and runs their OnCreate again. A helper that calls register for other code is one call site, so a second hook through it replaces the first silently, unless the helper passes its caller’s file and line on.

Hooks are configured and attached in registration order, which across packages is autolinking’s: packages sorted by name. A hook whose key turns on after the WebView was created attaches after the hooks attached already.

items.title: WebViewContext
items.text:
One WebView as one hook sees it, for the life of the WKWebView.

protocol WebViewContext : AnyObject

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Call emit(_:_:) and ask(_:_:_:) from any thread, and the rest on the main thread, where configure, attach, the handlers and the answers run.

A context kept after the view closed does nothing.

A hook is on while its extension’s options are not null or false; HookExtension.options says what off means. onOptionsChange(_:) still runs while it is off, so the hook can undo what it set up, and again when the hook turns on.

Values from JS arrive as Foundation’s JSON types: a number as NSNumber, an object as NSDictionary, null as nil (NSNull inside an array).

items.title: ask(_:_:_:)
items.text:
Sends the event as emit(_:_:) does, and calls onAnswer with the extension’s onEvent return value, a promise awaited.

func ask(_ name: String, _ payload: [String : Any], _ onAnswer: @escaping (Any?) -> Void)

items.title: Discussion
items.text: It answers nil when the handler throws or there is none, or when the Document ends first; there is no timeout. It answers nil at once while the hook is off, and after the view closed. An ask made before the first commit (in attach, or after a crash) belongs to the Document that commit opens.

items.title: emit(_:_:)
items.text:
Sends an event to JS as <key>.<name>: the extension’s onEvent gets { name, payload }, with name relative to the key. It is dropped while the hook is off, and after the view closed.

func emit(_ name: String, _ payload: [String : Any])

items.title: handle(_:_:)
items.text:
Answers JS’s ref.hook("<key>", method, args): handler gets the arguments and calls reply exactly once, and both cross as JSON.

func handle(_ method: String, _ handler: @escaping (_ args: [Any], _ reply: @escaping (Any?) -> Void) -> Void)

items.title: Discussion
items.text: One handler per method: the last one wins. A handler can’t fail: a reply JSON can’t encode rejects the JS call with native_error. A handler that never replies leaves the call waiting until the view unmounts: a navigation or a crash doesn’t settle it.

items.title: navigationDelegates
items.text:
Your navigation delegates, in order. While the hook is off, none of them gets a callback.

var navigationDelegates: [WKNavigationDelegate] { get set }

items.title: Discussion
items.text:
WebKit reads which callbacks a delegate implements when it is assigned, so a delegate must implement what it handles by the time you add it. The core assigns itself again after each change to the list.

Each callback reaches the delegates by one of these rules:

  • A decision, the action or the response policy, goes to the first delegate that implements it, instead of the core. Either action policy variant, with or without preferences, counts, and that delegate’s own variant is called.
  • The authentication challenge goes to each delegate that implements it, in order, until one answers other than .performDefaultHandling; when none does, WebKit’s default handling. Each must call its completion handler exactly once, and the next delegate gets the challenge only after that.
  • Every other callback the core implements reaches the core, then each delegate that implements it. So do didStartProvisionalNavigation and didReceiveServerRedirectForProvisionalNavigation.
  • Any other callback goes only to the first delegate that implements it.

Taking a decision switches off what the core decides from the app’s props or their defaults, the default navigation rules’ security checks included, and a core.warning names the callback and what stops applying. A delegate that takes the action policy decides navigations instead of the navigation rules, which still decide new windows unless a UI delegate takes createWebViewWith.

A decision more than one delegate implements still goes only to the first, and a core.warning names it. Each warning comes once per WebView, when the delegate is added.

While onDownload is set, a delegate whose didBecome sets download.delegate takes the download, and onDownload gets nothing for it.

items.title: onDestroyed(_:)
items.text:
Runs handler once this view closes, with DocumentEnd.closing, the only reason it gets on iOS.

func onDestroyed(_ handler: @escaping (DocumentEnd) -> Void)

items.title: Discussion
items.text:
It comes after the onDocumentEnd(_:) handlers that get closing. The WKWebView has stopped loading, paused its media and left the view by then, but is still alive, and the context does nothing.

Clean up here: what attach set up on the WKWebView, such as an observation or a swapped class.

items.title: onDocumentEnd(_:)
items.text:
Runs handler at each end of the Document (see DocumentEnd), after the core’s own resets: per-page state belongs here.

func onDocumentEnd(_ handler: @escaping (DocumentEnd) -> Void)

items.title: onOptionsChange(_:)
items.text:
Runs handler with this hook’s extension’s new options each time they change, live; nil when the hook turns off.

func onOptionsChange(_ handler: @escaping (Any?) -> Void)

items.title: options
items.text:
This hook’s extension’s options, the new ones after a change; nil while the hook is off.

var options: Any? { get }

items.title: refreshControl
items.text:
The control pullToRefresh shows: the same one for the view’s life, shown or not; nil once the view has closed.

var refreshControl: UIRefreshControl? { get }

items.title: Discussion
items.text: Style it (tintColor), but leave its actions and where it is shown to the core.

items.title: uiDelegates
items.text:
Your UI delegates, in order, by the rules of navigationDelegates.

var uiDelegates: [WKUIDelegate] { get set }

items.title: Discussion
items.text:
Their decisions are createWebViewWith, the alert, confirm and prompt panels and the media capture permission. webViewDidClose reaches every delegate.

A callback goes only to the list of the protocol that declares it: a navigation delegate’s alert panel, or a UI delegate’s action policy, is never called.

A delegate that holds a panel’s completion handler should set webView.accessibilityElementsHidden until it answers, as the core does for its own panels: an accessibility query (XCTest’s) into the blocked page hangs.

items.title: url
items.text:
The committed URL, the one useWebViewState reports; empty before the first commit.

var url: String { get }

items.title: Discussion
items.text: Inside onDocumentEnd(_:) it is still the page that ended.

items.title: @react-native-minimal-webview/extensions
items.text: Setup, each extension's platforms and how to vendor one are in the package's README.

items.title: Extensions
items.text:
One function per extension, whose result goes into the core's extensions prop.

  • androidLayerType

  • hideKeyboardAccessoryView

items.title: androidLayerType()
items.text:
androidLayerType(type): HookExtension | null

Android

Sets the WebView's layer type, and keeps it on the WebView that replaces one whose renderer crashed: react-native-webview's androidLayerType. Switched off, the layer type is 'none' again. Null on iOS.

items.title: basicAuthCredential()
items.text:
basicAuthCredential(credential): HookExtension

Answers HTTP auth challenges with credential, on every host: react-native-webview's basicAuthCredential.

iOS answers HTTP basic challenges, and Android every HTTP auth request, digest included. Neither sends the credential again once the site has rejected it: the site's 401 page shows. A change applies from the next challenge.

On iOS, a challenge it doesn't answer goes on to the native hooks' navigation delegates listed after it, then to WebKit's default handling.

A credential once accepted stays with the WebView's network session, as in a browser: after it changes or is switched off, an origin that accepted it can still get it, until the app restarts.

items.title: dialogs()
items.text:
dialogs(onDialog): HookExtension

Answers the page's alert, confirm and prompt with onDialog instead of the native dialogs; the page waits for the answer. Not in react-native-webview, whose dialogs are native.

The return value (a promise is awaited) is the answer: true accepts a confirm, a string is a prompt's text, and anything else, a throw too, dismisses the dialog (confirm false, prompt null). An alert's answer doesn't matter.

signal aborts when native stops waiting for the answer, and the dialog is then dismissed; HookExtension.onEvent has the rules.

Without this extension, the default dialogs show, as WebViewProps describes.

items.title: hideKeyboardAccessoryView()
items.text:
hideKeyboardAccessoryView(): HookExtension | null

iOS

Hides the bar above the keyboard (previous, next, done) for the page's inputs: react-native-webview's hideKeyboardAccessoryView. Null on Android.

It changes a private WebKit view, as react-native-webview does, so a WebKit update can stop it working.

items.title: menuItems()
items.text:
menuItems(menu): HookExtension | null

The text selection menu: react-native-webview's menuItems, suppressMenuItems and onCustomMenuSelection. items replace the system's items, onSelect gets the one chosen, and on iOS suppress hides system items. Null when neither is set on this platform (suppress alone on Android).

Turn it on when the WebView is created. Once it has, a change, switching it off included, applies to the next menu.

Its hook makes the WebView from a class of its own. When another hook's webViewClass or webViewFactory, registered earlier, makes it instead, there is no menu and the core warns.

items.title: nestedScrollEnabled()
items.text:
nestedScrollEnabled(): HookExtension | null

Android

Keeps a swipe that starts on the page for the page, inside a scrolling parent such as a ScrollView: react-native-webview's nestedScrollEnabled. Null on iOS.

android.webView.nestedScrollingEnabled doesn't do this: the parent still takes the swipe.

items.title: onScroll()
items.text:
onScroll(handler): HookExtension

Calls handler on each change of the scroll offset, with no throttling: react-native-webview's onScroll.

On iOS, the offsets include the content inset adjustment unless ios.scrollView.contentInsetAdjustmentBehavior is never, react-native-webview's default.

items.title: AndroidLayerType
items.text:
AndroidLayerType = "none" | "software" | "hardware"

Android

A layer type of Android's View.setLayerType, for androidLayerType.

The URL of the page (iOS: of the frame) that opened it.
