items.title: WebView()
items.text:
WebView(props): Element

A WebView whose native side decides navigations and owns the navigation state: see WebViewProps and WebViewRef.

items.title: createBridge()
items.text:
createBridge<Methods, Events>(options): Bridge<Methods, Events>

Creates a Bridge to the pages of allowedOrigins, for one WebView's bridge prop.

The type arguments type the method names, params, results and event payloads of call, handle, emit and on; nothing checks them at runtime, so a handler still validates what an untrusted page sends. Throws an Error for an invalid origin rule or timeout.

items.title: createWebViewRef()
items.text:
createWebViewRef(): WebViewRefObject

A ref to pass as a WebView's ref, made outside React (a module, a store) so code outside React can use it.

items.title: useWebViewState()
items.text:
useWebViewState(ref): NavigationState

The navigation state of the WebView mounted with ref (a useRef, createRef or createWebViewRef one); re-renders on every change, and follows a remount.

items.title: WebViewProps
items.text:
What the WebView loads, its settings, and the callbacks for its events and the page's requests.

The ones from React Native's ViewProps (style, testID, nativeID, the accessibility props, layout and touch events) go to the native view.

Every on… callback is read when its event or request comes, so adding, changing or removing one applies to the next, and a request without one gets the default described on its prop. One that answers a request and throws (or rejects) is logged with console.error and gives the refusing answer: onNavigationRequest block, onOpenExternal null (the core opens nothing), onFileRequest cancel, onPermissionRequest deny, an extension's onEvent null.

The signal such a callback gets aborts when native stops waiting for its answer (the page moved on, crashed or unmounted), and a late answer is dropped.

JS dialogs (alert, confirm, prompt) and HTTP auth have no prop. iOS shows a UIAlertController titled with the frame's host, one at a time (one that comes while another shows is cancelled), and Android WebView's own dialogs. An auth challenge is cancelled on Android, and gets WebKit's default handling on iOS: without a stored credential, the site's 401 page shows. dialogs and basicAuthCredential of @react-native-minimal-webview/extensions take them over, or a native hook does.

items.title: android?
items.text:
optional android?: AndroidSettings

Android

Android settings by setter name; see AndroidSettings.

items.title: bridge?
items.text:
optional bridge?: Bridge<BridgeMethodMap, BridgeEventMap>

The bridge to the page, from createBridge.

Read when the WebView is created: another bridge recreates it (the page reloads and the navigation state starts over), so make it once (useMemo). A bridge serves one mounted WebView at a time: attaching it to a second throws.

On Android with a WebView older than 101 there is no bridge: calls reject with unavailable, and a warning says so, once per process.

items.title: extensions?
items.text:
optional extensions?: readonly (false | HookExtension | null | undefined)[]

The native hooks to turn on, as HookExtensions: a package with a native hook exports a function that returns one.

A false, null or undefined entry is left out, so on && extension(…) switches one on and off; see HookExtension.options for what off means. A hook attaches when its key first appears, and a later change of its options reaches it live, without recreating the WebView. A key turned on after the WebView was created attaches its hook then, unless the hook has a configure step or its own WebView class (webViewClass, webViewFactory): that one attaches only when the WebView is created, and a warning says so.

items.title: injectedScripts?
items.text:
optional injectedScripts?: InjectedScript[]

Scripts to run at document start, before the page's own, in the frames picked by each script's allFrames and origins.

A change applies from the next navigation. On Android with a WebView older than 101 they don't run (a warning says so, once per process).

items.title: ios?
items.text:
optional ios?: IOSSettings

iOS

WebKit settings by property name; see IOSSettings.

items.title: navigationRules?
items.text:
optional navigationRules?: readonly NavigationRule[]

Which navigations load in place, open externally or are blocked, decided natively; the first matching rule wins, and with no match the navigation is blocked.

Unset, the rules are defaultNavigationRules; [] is no rules, so every navigation they decide is blocked.

about:, blob:, data: and javascript: always load in place.

The source load, reloads and back/forward skip the rules; a redirect of the source load doesn't, nor on Android a redirect of a reload or back/forward. The rules never see a form POST, on either platform: it loads in place, and one to a new window loads in place on iOS, and on Android isn't shown (the request may still reach the server).

An external intent: URL (Android) opens only as a browsable intent, without its explicit component or selector; when no app handles it, an http(s) S.browser_fallback_url goes through the rules (main frame, no user gesture), and the intent: itself is reported as block.

A change applies from the next navigation.

A native hook can take these decisions, defaults included: see WebViewContext.clients (Android) and navigationDelegates (iOS).

items.title: Example
items.text:
<WebView
  source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }}
  // myapp: opens externally even without a user gesture; everything else as by default
  navigationRules={[{ scheme: ['myapp'], action: 'external' }, ...defaultNavigationRules]}
/>

items.title: onDownload?
items.text:
optional onDownload?: (result) => void

A download finished (Download) or failed (DownloadFailure).

With this prop the core saves the file: iOS downloads it in the page's session; Android fetches it again with the host's cookies (whatever their SameSite) and the page's user agent. That fetch sends no POST body, source headers or HTTP auth, so a download that needs them can fail, or save the server's login page as the file, and it fails above 100 MB, on a redirect off https, and for blob: on a WebView older than 83.

Without this prop, an http(s) download opens externally (onOpenExternal or the system browser, without the page's session), and a data: or blob: one is dropped. A PDF is a download on Android; iOS shows it inline.

On iOS a file response is a download only in the main frame; an <a download> link is one from any frame.

On Android a native hook's WebViewContext.onDownloadStart is offered each download first, and one it takes reaches neither this prop nor the external fallback.

items.title: onError?
items.text:
optional onError?: (event) => void

A main-frame load failed, or got an HTTP error status.

After a failed load iOS keeps the page before it on screen, and Android shows WebView's own error page. On Android with a WebView older than 146, an SSL error on a back/forward load isn't reported.

A renderer crash isn't reported here: it makes the cut-off load's outcome failed and calls onProcessGone.

items.title: onFileRequest?
items.text:
optional onFileRequest?: (request, signal) => string[] | Promise<string[] | null> | null

Android

Answers <input type="file"> with file:// or content:// URIs, or null to cancel.

Without it, the system file chooser opens, one at a time for the whole app, and ignores capture: a request while one is open is cancelled, and if the chooser's activity died without returning a result, so is every request until the app restarts.

iOS always shows WebKit's picker, which needs NSCameraUsageDescription and NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription.

Until the answer settles, the page's next file request waits.

items.title: onFullscreenChange?
items.text:
optional onFullscreenChange?: (event) => void

Android

The page entered or left fullscreen (active).

Fullscreen works without it: the page's view covers the window, the system bars hide and back exits. iOS shows WebKit's own fullscreen, not reported.

items.title: onLoadEnd?
items.text:
optional onLoadEnd?: (state) => void

loading went false: state.outcome says how the load ended.

items.title: onLoadStart?
items.text:
optional onLoadStart?: (state) => void

loading went true.

On Android with a WebView older than 146, a load that never commits fires neither this nor onLoadEnd.

items.title: onNavigation?
items.text:
optional onNavigation?: (event) => void

Every navigation the rules, or their defaults, decided.

Not reported: the source load, reloads, back/forward, and a navigation a native hook decides.

items.title: onNavigationRequest?
items.text:
optional onNavigationRequest?: (request, signal) => NavigationAction | Promise<NavigationAction>

Decides each navigation an ask rule matches, within 1 s.

A late, missing or other answer is block, as is one still pending when another page commits; signal aborts at the timeout and at that commit. Without this prop, ask is block. Until the next commit, a URL it allowed isn't asked again on a redirect back to it (Android), or when the same kind of frame loads it again (iOS).

items.title: onNavigationStateChange?
items.text:
optional onNavigationStateChange?: (state) => void

Every change to the navigation state.

Changes that arrive together may be combined into one call; loading going true is never combined away, so a load that starts and fails at once still reports both.

items.title: onOpenExternal?
items.text:
optional onOpenExternal?: (request, signal) => boolean | void | Promise<boolean | void>

Opens external navigations, every one, an Android intent: URL included, before onNavigation reports them.

Return false (a promise is awaited) to hand it back: the core then opens it as it does without this prop, an intent:'s fallback URL included. Any other answer, undefined too, means you opened it. When signal aborts, nothing opens it.

Without this prop, the system browser or app for the URL opens it, without asking canOpenURL first, so no LSApplicationQueriesSchemes (iOS) or <queries> (Android) entries are needed.

items.title: onPermissionRequest?
items.text:
optional onPermissionRequest?: (request, signal) => boolean | Promise<boolean>

Camera, microphone and, on Android, location and protected media (DRM) for the main frame.

Answer true to grant, having asked the OS first (expo-camera, expo-location): without OS permission the page's request fails anyway. On iOS, true also skips WebKit's own prompt.

Without this prop, Android denies and iOS shows WebKit's prompt (location always does). iOS needs NSCameraUsageDescription and NSMicrophoneUsageDescription, Android the CAMERA and RECORD_AUDIO manifest permissions. Android keeps a location answer until the page changes.

Anything but true denies. signal also aborts when Android withdraws the request. Until the answer settles, the page's next request of the same kind waits.

items.title: onProcessGone?
items.text:
optional onProcessGone?: (event) => void

The renderer died; see ProcessGoneEvent for the recovery.

Android's WebViews share one renderer, so each of them reports its death.

items.title: pullToRefresh?
items.text:
optional pullToRefresh?: boolean = false

Pull down at the top of the page to reload: UIRefreshControl on iOS, SwipeRefreshLayout on Android, where a pull inside a scrolled inner scroller (overflow: auto) scrolls it instead.

It reloads as reload() does, a POST source included. A change applies at once.

items.title: ref?
items.text:
optional ref?: Ref<WebViewRef>

Gets the WebViewRef.

Give each mounted WebView its own ref: one shared by two points at the last mounted (with a warning in development), and can turn null when either unmounts.

items.title: sharedCookies?
items.text:
optional sharedCookies?: boolean = false

iOS

Copies HTTPCookieStorage (native requests) into the WebView before each source load, which waits for it, and the WebView's cookie changes, deletions included, back as they happen.

Android needs nothing: CookieManager is shared app-wide, and flushed when the app goes to the background.

items.title: source
items.text:
source: WebViewSource

What to load.

A new source loads at once, unless it equals the loaded one field by field: that loads nothing, even after the page navigated away.

items.title: userAgent?
items.text:
optional userAgent?: string

Replaces the whole user agent, over ios.webView.customUserAgent and android.settings.userAgentString. Without it, those keys apply; unset, they are the platform's own user agent.

To append to the default one instead, set ios.configuration.applicationNameForUserAgent and, on Android, android.settings.userAgentString to WebView.android.defaultUserAgent plus your suffix.

A change applies from the next navigation.

items.title: IOSConstants
items.text:
iOS

WebKit's and UIScrollView's enums and option sets by raw value, for the iOS keys that take one: configuration: { dataDetectorTypes: IOSConstants.DataDetectorTypes.link }.

An option set's all is the OR of its listed bits, not NSUIntegerMax, which JSON can't carry. WebsiteDataType has the data type names the websiteDataStore methods take, for call; WebViewDataType is the option set webView.fetchDataOfTypes: takes.

items.title: android
items.text:
Android

Android's process-wide WebView functions. On iOS they do nothing, and defaultUserAgent is null.

items.title: preconnect()
items.text:
preconnect(url): void

Android

Opens a connection to url's origin (DNS, TCP, TLS) in WebView's default profile, ahead of a load that comes later.

Use it for a load that hasn't started yet: as the screen with the WebView is pushed, or for the next page a mounted WebView will go to. A WebView connects to its source itself as it mounts, so preconnecting source at mount gains nothing.

It starts WebView on the UI thread if nothing has yet, so call it once warmUp() has had time or a WebView is mounted.

Needs the androidx.webkit features MULTI_PROFILE and ENQUEUE_PRECONNECT or PRECONNECT; without them it does nothing. For prefetch and prerender, a native hook uses ProfileStore.

items.title: setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled()
items.text:
setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(enabled): void

Android

Turns remote debugging (chrome://inspect) of every WebView in the app on or off.

Until it is called, it is on when the app is debuggable (a debug build) and off otherwise. Called before any WebView exists, it applies when the first one is made, so it doesn't start WebView. On iOS, ios.webView.inspectable sets it per WebView.

items.title: warmUp()
items.text:
warmUp(): void

Android

Starts WebView before any WebView mounts, so the first WebView mounts sooner.

It helps only if it runs well before the first WebView mounts: at app start, or as the screen with the WebView is pushed. Calling it at mount gains nothing. WebView starts once per app, and React Native's first fetch starts it too.

items.title: defaultUserAgent
items.text:
defaultUserAgent: string | null

Android

Android's default user agent, for android.settings.userAgentString with a suffix.

The first read loads WebView's code, on the JS thread: read it once warmUp() has had time or a WebView is mounted.

items.title: AndroidSettingKeys
items.text:
AndroidSettingKeys = object

Android

The Android settings keys by root: the one-argument WebSettings, WebView and CookieManager setters, then WebSettingsCompat's and WebViewCompat's statics, then the scroll setters WebView inherits from View.

@since is the API level. A key a newer SDK or androidx.webkit adds goes under the root's other.

items.title: AndroidSettings
items.text:
AndroidSettings = object

Android

Android settings by setter name without set.

Any public setter works, including ones a newer SDK or androidx.webkit adds (under a root's other). The keys the SDK lists autocomplete, with their @since; the constants are in AndroidConstants.

A key with no public setter for the value's type, or one this device's WebView lacks, is skipped with a warning; nothing here can crash the app. A root's default keys are the package's, and yours go over them; a key the package doesn't set keeps the platform's default (acceptThirdPartyCookies is off, for one). A key you remove goes back to the value it had before you first set it; one with no getter, such as geolocationEnabled, keeps its value until the WebView is recreated, with a warning.

The ref's get and call take these roots, plus cookieManager and webStorage; a key is the getter's name without get or is.

items.title: Example
items.text:
<WebView
  source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }}
  android={{
    settings: { textZoom: 120, cacheMode: AndroidConstants.WebSettings.LOAD_NO_CACHE },
    webView: { overScrollMode: 2 },
  }}
/>

items.title: settings?
items.text:
optional settings?: SettingsRoot<AndroidSettingKeys["settings"]> = { userAgentString: null }

WebSettings setters, then static WebSettingsCompat ones.

Each new WebView starts with javaScriptEnabled, domStorageEnabled, supportMultipleWindows and builtInZoomControls on; allowFileAccess, allowContentAccess, displayZoomControls and downloadFaviconsEnabled off; mixedContentMode MIXED_CONTENT_NEVER_ALLOW; and, with WebView 146 and newer, backForwardCacheEnabled on. userAgentString: null is WebView's default user agent.

items.title: webView?
items.text:
optional webView?: SettingsRoot<AndroidSettingKeys["webView"]>

WebView setters (static and inherited View ones too), then WebViewCompat ones, then CookieManager's acceptThirdPartyCookies.

webContentsDebuggingEnabled is refused: it is process-wide, set with WebView.android.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled.

items.title: Bridge<Methods, Events>
items.text:
Bridge<Methods, Events> = object

A promise-based RPC channel to window.nativeBridge in the page.

Attach it with the bridge prop. Handlers and listeners belong to the bridge, not to a WebView: they stay across unmounts. Messages have no size limit.

What it sends waits for the page's DOMContentLoaded, so the handlers and listeners of the page's synchronous and deferred scripts are in place, and never reaches a later page, even one on the same origin. The page's own calls don't wait: one made before React Native has registered its method rejects with not_found.

A call or event made while no WebView is mounted with the bridge waits the same way. A call's timeout runs meanwhile, and only the latest 1000 are kept: an older call rejects with unavailable. Unmounting rejects the calls in flight with navigated.

The page's window.nativeBridge has the same four methods, call(method, params?, { timeoutMs? }), handle, emit and on, and its calls reject with a CodedError.

items.title: call()
items.text:
call<M>(method, params?, options?): Promise<Methods[M]["result"]>

Calls a method the page registered with nativeBridge.handle.

Rejects with a CodedError: timeout, not_found, handler_error, navigated or unavailable. timeoutMs overrides the bridge's for this call, and one that isn't 0 or more rejects with a plain RangeError.

items.title: emit()
items.text:
emit<E>(event, payload?): void

Fires an event the page listens to with nativeBridge.on.

Dropped if the page goes away before it arrives, or if the page has no listener for it.

items.title: handle()
items.text:
handle<M>(method, handler): () => void

Answers nativeBridge.call(method, params) from the page.

One handler per method: a later one replaces it. Returns an unsubscribe function, which removes only this handler.

items.title: on()
items.text:
on<E>(event, listener): () => void

Listens to nativeBridge.emit(event, payload) from the page. Returns an unsubscribe function.

A listener that throws is reported as an unhandled promise rejection, and the event's later listeners don't run.

items.title: [CONNECTION]
items.text:
readonly [CONNECTION]: BridgeConnection

What <WebView> attaches to. Only createBridge sets it, so a hand-made or mock Bridge doesn't type-check.

items.title: BridgeEventMap
items.text:
BridgeEventMap = Record<string, unknown>

The events either side may emit, for createBridge<Methods, Events>.

With a map, emit and on take only its events: another name doesn't compile.

items.title: Example
items.text:
type Events = { themeChanged: 'light' | 'dark' };
const bridge = createBridge<Methods, Events>({ allowedOrigins: ['https://example.com'] });

items.title: BridgeHandler<Params, Result>
items.text:
BridgeHandler<Params, Result> = (params, sender) => Result | Promise<Result>

Answers a bridge call: the return value (a promise is awaited) is the result.

A throw or rejection rejects the call with `handler_error` and the error's message.

items.title: BridgeMethodMap
items.text:
BridgeMethodMap = Record<string, { params?: unknown; result?: unknown; }>

The methods either side may call, for createBridge<Methods>.

One map covers both directions, so a method is named once, whichever side handles it. With a map, handle and call take only its methods: another name doesn't compile. A type, not an interface (an interface has no index signature, so it doesn't satisfy Record).

items.title: Example
items.text:
type Methods = { share: { params: { url: string }; result: boolean } };
const bridge = createBridge<Methods>({ allowedOrigins: ['https://example.com'] });

items.title: allowedOrigins
items.text:
allowedOrigins: string[]

The origins whose pages get window.nativeBridge, main frame only: an origin, a *. wildcard that matches subdomains only (not the domain itself), an IP literal, or '*' for any origin, opaque ones too.

Each takes an optional port. http or https, no path, ASCII (punycode) hosts; case is ignored, and a missing port means 80 or 443.

items.title: timeoutMs?
items.text:
optional timeoutMs?: number = 10000

Per-call timeout in milliseconds, also the default for the page's nativeBridge.call; 0 or Infinity means none.

items.title: BridgeSender
items.text:
BridgeSender = object

Who sent a call or event: the page's origin as location.origin writes it (https://example.com:8443), checked by native code, not taken from the page.

Every allowed origin gets the same trust; a handler scopes itself with this.

items.title: CGPoint
items.text:
CGPoint = object

iOS

An iOS struct the settings channel carries as an object.

items.title: CGRect
items.text:
CGRect = object

iOS

An iOS struct the settings channel carries as an object.

items.title: CGSize
items.text:
CGSize = object

iOS

An iOS struct the settings channel carries as an object.

items.title: CodedError
items.text:
CodedError = Error & object

What a ref method or a bridge call rejects with: an Error whose code says why.

items.title: filename
items.text:
filename: string

A plain file name, no path, but the page chose it, like the content and mimeType: don't open the file as trusted.

items.title: uri
items.text:
uri: string

A file:// in the app's cache (iOS: the temporary directory), which the core never deletes.

items.title: url
items.text:
url: string | null

The server URL the file came from; null when the page generated it (data: or blob: URL).

items.title: DownloadFailure
items.text:
DownloadFailure = { description: string; filename: string; kind: "network" | "data"; ok: false; url: string | null; } | { filename: string; kind: "http"; ok: false; statusCode: number; url: string; }

A download that could not be saved; kind says why.

  • network: connecting or reading the response failed, or a redirect was refused.
  • http: the response had an error status (Android only: iOS saves what the server sent).
  • data: the content: a bad data: or blob: URL, the page not reading its blob, an unsupported scheme, or (Android) a file above 100 MB or a blob: URL the main frame can't read (a cross-origin iframe's, or one already revoked).

items.title: ErrorCode
items.text:
ErrorCode = "timeout" | "not_found" | "handler_error" | "script_error" | "native_error" | "navigated" | "unavailable"

Why a ref method or a bridge call rejected. Each code means the same on every method that rejects with it.

  • timeout: a bridge call got no answer in time.
  • not_found: nothing by that name answers: no bridge handler for the method, no attached hook name that is on and handles method, or no such root, key, method (on Android, one that takes these arguments) or selector (on this OS or WebView version too; a private _ key of an iOS get too), or a malformed path.
  • handler_error: the handler of a bridge call, on either side, failed; the message is its error's.
  • script_error: evaluate's script threw, rejected or didn't parse.
  • native_error: the platform refused or failed the call: a member the core owns (or a private selector for an iOS call), a key get can't read, wrong arguments (iOS), a completion handler call can't await, a native exception or NSError, or a result JSON can't carry (NaN).
  • navigated: the page or the WebView went away while the call was pending (a navigation, a crash, an unmount), so it may have run: retry only what is safe to repeat.
  • unavailable: the call didn't run: the WebView is gone or not mounted yet, is being rebuilt after its renderer died (Android), the bridge's queue was full and dropped it, or lacks the feature (the method's TSDoc names the Android System WebView it needs, or a compat method this WebView doesn't support).

A programming error, such as an argument of the wrong type, can reject with a plain TypeError instead.

items.title: accept
items.text:
accept: string[]

Its accept list as written: MIME types and extensions (.pdf).

items.title: capture
items.text:
capture: boolean

Its capture attribute: the page wants the camera.

items.title: HookEvent<N, P>
items.text:
HookEvent<N, P> = object

An event a native hook sent with emit or ask.

items.title: N
items.text:
N extends string = string

The event's name, to type one hook's events.

items.title: name
items.text:
name: N

The event's name, relative to the extension's key: pageLoaded for 'pageCounter.pageLoaded'.

items.title: HookExtension
items.text:
HookExtension = object

A native hook's JS side, for WebViewProps.extensions: its key, its options, and what takes its events.

A package with a native hook exports a function that returns one, so that an app turns the hook on by putting it in extensions.

items.title: key
items.text:
key: string

The key the hook is registered under.

A key no hook is registered under warns: pass a one-platform hook's extension on that platform only. Two extensions with one key warn in development, and the later one wins.

items.title: onEvent?
items.text:
optional onEvent?: (event, signal?) => unknown

Each of the hook's events, with name relative to key: it goes to the extension whose key its name starts with ('<key>.'; the longest key, when several do), and one no extension owns is dropped. For an ask, the return value (a promise is awaited) is the answer, and undefined answers null. signal is set only for an ask, and aborts when native stops waiting for the answer: an ask has no timeout, but one still open when the page goes away is answered null.

The latest onEvent always takes the events: a render with new handlers sends native nothing.

items.title: options?
items.text:
optional options?: unknown = true

What the hook gets as its options. Null or false switches the hook off, as does leaving its extension out of extensions: it stays attached and gets null, but the core routes none of its delegates, clients or listeners, drops its events, answers its asks with null, and rejects ref.hook calls to its handlers with not_found. Undefined means true. Turning it on again gives it the new options.

items.title: IOSPrivateSettingKeys
items.text:
IOSPrivateSettingKeys = object

iOS

The private WebKit settings IOSSettings takes besides IOSSettingKeys, both off by default.

items.title: allowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs?
items.text:
optional allowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs?: boolean

Lets a file: page read any URL.

items.title: allowFileAccessFromFileURLs?
items.text:
optional allowFileAccessFromFileURLs?: boolean

Lets a file: page read other file: URLs.

items.title: IOSSettingKeys
items.text:
IOSSettingKeys = object

iOS

The iOS settings keys by root: the writable WebKit and UIScrollView properties the settings channel can carry, from the SDK headers.

@since is the iOS version. A key a newer SDK adds goes under the root's other.

items.title: Deprecated
items.text: This property is ignored; selection granularity is always character.

items.title: Deprecated
items.text: Use WKWebpagePreferences.allowsContentJavaScript to disable content JavaScript on a per-navigation basis

items.title: IOSSettings
items.text:
IOSSettings = object

iOS

WebKit settings by Objective-C property name.

Any public property works, including ones this package has never heard of (under a root's other). The keys the SDK headers list autocomplete, with their @since, as do the IOSPrivateSettingKeys. A value must fit the property's type: enums and option sets by raw value (from IOSConstants), structs as objects, a UIColor as #rrggbb or #rrggbbaa, an NSURL as a string, websiteDataStore as 'default' or 'nonPersistent'.

A key that doesn't fit, a private (_) one, or one the device's iOS lacks (its @since is newer) is skipped with a warning; nothing here can crash the app. So is a property UIKit declares without runtime metadata, such as webView.opaque: set it with call('webView.setOpaque:', [false]).

A root's default keys are the package's, and yours go over them; a key the package doesn't set keeps WebKit's default, and a key you remove goes back to the value it had before you first set it. The ref's get and call take these roots, plus websiteDataStore and httpCookieStore.

WebKit has no mixed-content setting: it applies its own policy.

items.title: Example
items.text:
<WebView
  source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }}
  ios={{
    configuration: { dataDetectorTypes: IOSConstants.DataDetectorTypes.link },
    scrollView: { bounces: false, contentInset: { top: 0, left: 0, bottom: 80, right: 0 } },
  }}
/>

items.title: configuration?
items.text:
optional configuration?: SettingsRoot<IOSSettingKeys["configuration"] & IOSPrivateSettingKeys["configuration"]> = { allowsInlineMediaPlayback: true }

WKWebViewConfiguration: read once, when the WKWebView is created; a change recreates the WebView (the page reloads and the navigation state starts over). It is a copy, so call on it changes nothing.

items.title: webpagePreferences?
items.text:
optional webpagePreferences?: SettingsRoot<IOSSettingKeys["webpagePreferences"]>

WKWebpagePreferences (configuration.defaultWebpagePreferences), live from the next navigation.

items.title: webView?
items.text:
optional webView?: SettingsRoot<IOSSettingKeys["webView"]> = { customUserAgent: null, inspectable: __DEV__ }

The WKWebView, live.

customUserAgent: null is WebKit's default user agent, with applicationNameForUserAgent appended.

items.title: InjectedScript
items.text:
InjectedScript = object

Runs at document start, before any page script and before the DOM is parsed.

items.title: allFrames?
items.text:
optional allFrames?: boolean = false

Runs it in every frame, iframes included.

items.title: origins
items.text:
origins: string[]

The origins whose frames run it, in the syntax of BridgeOptions.allowedOrigins. Each frame is matched by its own location.origin, so a listed page's iframes from other origins don't run it; about:blank and srcdoc frames have their parent's origin. '*' matches every origin, opaque ones (data:, sandboxed frames) and file: included; [] matches none.

Without '*' in the list, the code runs inside a function: its top-level let, const, class, function and var stay local to it, so put what the page should see on window. An invalid rule throws when the WebView renders.

items.title: LoadErrorEvent
items.text:
LoadErrorEvent = { code: number; description: string; kind: "network" | "ssl"; url: string; } | { kind: "http"; statusCode: number; url: string; }

A main-frame error, for onError.

  • network and ssl: the load failed, no page arrived; an SSL error always cancels the load. code is the platform's own: on iOS the NSError code (an NSURLError* constant, usually), on Android WebViewClient.ERROR_* for network and SslError.SSL_* for ssl.
  • http: the response had an HTTP error status (400+), and the site's own error page shows.

items.title: NavigationAction
items.text:
NavigationAction = "allow" | "block" | "external"

What happens to a navigation.

  • allow: it loads in place, on iOS a tapped universal link too (instead of opening the app that claims it).
  • block: it is cancelled.
  • external: onOpenExternal, or else the system, opens it.

items.title: action
items.text:
action: NavigationAction

Without onOpenExternal, or when it returns false, an external URL that no app opens is reported as block.

items.title: rule
items.text:
rule: number | null

Index of the matching rule in navigationRules, or in defaultNavigationRules when that is unset; null when no rule decided (none matched, a scheme that always loads in place or is always blocked, or a download opened externally).

items.title: NavigationRequest
items.text:
NavigationRequest = object

A navigation an ask rule puts to onNavigationRequest, or an external one to onOpenExternal.

items.title: mainFrame
items.text:
mainFrame: boolean

Whether it's the main frame's, not an iframe's.

items.title: NavigationRule
items.text:
NavigationRule = object

A pattern over a navigation's URL and kind, and what the navigations it matches do.

Every field it sets must match; for a list, one matching entry is enough. A field left out matches anything; a flag set to false matches only the requests without it.

items.title: Example
items.text:
const navigationRules: NavigationRule[] = [
  { query: ['gad_source', 'utm_term=google'], action: 'block' }, // gad_source with any value, utm_term only =google
  { scheme: ['tel', 'mailto'], action: 'external' },
  { host: ['*.example.com'], path: ['/checkout'], action: 'external' }, // shop.example.com/checkouts too
  { host: ['example.com', '*.example.com'], action: 'allow' }, // *.example.com alone skips example.com
];

items.title: action
items.text:
action: NavigationAction | "ask"

What the navigations it matches do; ask puts each to onNavigationRequest.

On Android, which can't hold a navigation until JS answers, it works only for the main frame (elsewhere it is block): the navigation is cancelled, and an allowed one loads again after the answer, without the page's referrer policy or the gesture flag.

items.title: host?
items.text:
optional host?: string[]

Hosts: exact, or a *. suffix wildcard that matches subdomains only, not the domain itself.

Case, port, userinfo and a trailing dot are ignored.

items.title: mainFrame?
items.text:
optional mainFrame?: boolean

The main frame's navigation (true) or an iframe's (false).

Android decides only an iframe's non-http(s) navigations, so a mainFrame: false rule for http(s) is iOS only.

items.title: newWindow?
items.text:
optional newWindow?: boolean

A target=_blank or window.open navigation, always a main-frame one.

An allowed one loads in place: there is never a second WebView, so no window.opener (a native hook that takes createWebViewWith on iOS or onCreateWindow on Android owns real popups).

One to data:, blob:, javascript:, about: or file: is always blocked (on Android, WebView may still run a javascript: one's script, with the page's origin), and one opened with no URL (window.open('')) is decided by the URL the page sends it to within 5 s, and dropped otherwise.

One opened without a user gesture reaches the rules only with javaScriptCanOpenWindowsAutomatically on (ios.preferences, android.settings; off by default); otherwise WebKit or WebView drops it unreported.

items.title: path?
items.text:
optional path?: string[]

Path prefixes: plain prefixes of the percent-encoded URL path, not whole segments.

A URL without an authority (myapp:/open) has the path /.

items.title: query?
items.text:
optional query?: string[]

Query parameters, percent-encoded as in the URL and case-sensitive: a name matches that parameter whatever its value, and name=value only that exact value.

items.title: scheme?
items.text:
optional scheme?: string[]

URL schemes without the : (tel), exact and case-insensitive.

items.title: userInitiated?
items.text:
optional userInitiated?: boolean

A user gesture started it.

A location.href change or window.open from a click handler is true on Android, but false on iOS, where only a tapped link is. A redirect of a load the core starts itself (an allowed new window, and on Android an allowed ask) is never user-initiated.

items.title: NavigationState
items.text:
NavigationState = object

A WebView's navigation state, as native reports it: from useWebViewState and onNavigationStateChange.

While no WebView is mounted it is the initial state: url and title empty, pendingUrl and outcome null, loading, canGoBack and canGoForward false, progress 0.

items.title: outcome
items.text:
outcome: "finished" | "failed" | "cancelled" | null

How the last main-frame load ended; null while one is loading, and before the first.

  • failed: a network or SSL error, or a renderer crash, cut it off.
  • cancelled: it never showed a page (a stop before the response, a download, a 204, a redirect the rules blocked, a load a newer one replaced); a stop after the page arrived is cancelled on iOS but finished on Android, and a 204 is finished on iOS 17.

An HTTP error status (404) is finished: the site's page shows, and onError gets an http error. On Android with a WebView older than 146, a load that never commits changes nothing here.

items.title: pendingUrl
items.text:
pendingUrl: string | null

A main-frame load in progress, which may still fail or be blocked.

Iframes never change it. Always null on Android with a WebView older than 146.

items.title: url
items.text:
url: string

The page on screen: changes on commit and same-document navigation (pushState, replaceState, hash), and stays the old page while a load is in progress.

After a failed load, the failed URL. Iframes never change it.

items.title: PermissionRequest
items.text:
PermissionRequest = object

A page's permission request, for onPermissionRequest.

Only the main frame asks (on Android, which doesn't name the frame, any frame of the top page's origin); other frames, and a page with an opaque origin (data:, a sandboxed frame), are denied without asking.

items.title: origin
items.text:
origin: string

The requesting page's origin, as location.origin writes it; every file: page is file://.

items.title: PermissionResource
items.text:
PermissionResource = "camera" | "microphone" | "geolocation" | "protectedMedia"

A device resource a page can ask for.

geolocation and protectedMedia (the device id DRM playback needs, Widevine) are Android only: on iOS, location always shows WebKit's own prompt, and FairPlay asks nothing.

items.title: didCrash
items.text:
didCrash: boolean | null

Whether the renderer crashed (true) or the system killed it for memory (false); null on iOS, where WebKit doesn't say.

Test it with === true or === false, not as a condition.

items.title: recovered
items.text:
recovered: boolean

Whether the core reloads the page: on iOS in place; on Android in a new WebView, once the app is in the foreground and the view on screen, with the history restored unless the source page was on screen, and with the props applied but not what call set.

False while a POST source is on screen, which, as in a browser, isn't sent again unasked (reload() sends it), and after more than 3 crashes in 60 s, counted for the whole app on Android, until the next reload() (on iOS also a source change); pull-to-refresh doesn't lift it.

items.title: SettingValue
items.text:
SettingValue = boolean | number | string | null | UIEdgeInsets | CGPoint | CGSize | CGRect

What a platform setting can take: what its property or setter accepts. An object is one of the iOS structs.

items.title: SettingsRoot<Keys>
items.text:
SettingsRoot<Keys> = Keys & object

A settings root: its generated keys (IOSSettingKeys, AndroidSettingKeys, from the SDK headers), so a misspelled key fails to compile, and other for the keys they lack.

items.title: other?
items.text:
optional other?: Record<string, SettingValue | undefined> & { [K in keyof Keys]?: never }

Any other key the platform has (a newer SDK's, one the headers don't list), untyped. It is set as if it were at the root; a generated key can't go here.

items.title: UIEdgeInsets
items.text:
UIEdgeInsets = object

iOS

An iOS struct the settings channel carries as an object.

items.title: WebViewRef
items.text:
WebViewRef = object

The methods a WebView's ref gets: navigation, scripts, and platform and hook calls.

A handle kept after its WebView unmounted is safe to call: the navigation methods do nothing, and evaluate, get, call and hook reject with unavailable. One still pending when the WebView unmounts rejects with navigated.

Those four wait up to about a second for a WebView that has just mounted (on Android, a call from the parent's first effect can come before the view exists), then reject with unavailable; in the background they don't wait.

items.title: call()
items.text:
call(method, args?): Promise<unknown>

Calls a platform method, root.method, and resolves with its result through JSON. It acts on the WebView as it is when the call arrives: a navigation doesn't reject it.

The roots are those of IOSSettings and AndroidSettings. On Android method is a public method of the root's object; on iOS an Objective-C selector.

Rejects with a CodedError: not_found, unavailable (Android) or native_error.

The core owns, and so rejects:

  • iOS: every selector that loads, navigates (setInteractionState: too), runs a script, starts a download or sets a delegate, and private (_), KVC, willChange…, didChange…, performSelector, init…, copy…, mutable…, new… and reference-counting selectors.
  • Android (in get too): the loads, navigations, clients, JavaScript interfaces, web message listeners, document-start scripts, the touch, scroll-change and navigation listeners, destroy, removeAllViews, pauseTimers, resumeTimers, evaluateJavascript and remote debugging (WebView.android.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled).

A trailing completion handler (iOS) or ValueCallback (Android) is left out of args: the call resolves with what it reports, or on iOS rejects with its error. On iOS, a selector whose completion handler isn't in this package's SDK headers, or reports something other than an object, an error or an integer, rejects with native_error. On Android, a method that takes args as they are wins over one that also takes a callback, and a null in the callback's place passes none.

One mistake the signature can't catch crashes the app: on iOS an object argument of the wrong class, and on Android a null listener or callback other than the trailing ValueCallback, once WebView calls it. For a method that takes another object, write a native hook.

items.title: args?
items.text:
unknown[]

The method's arguments: booleans, numbers, strings and null. On iOS also the structs as objects, and { set: [...] }, { date: seconds }, { data: base64 } or { cookie: properties } for an NSSet, NSDate, NSData or NSHTTPCookie; any other string stays an NSString. A cookie's properties are NSHTTPCookie's keys: Name, Value, Domain and Path are required; Max-Age (seconds, as a string), Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite are some of the optional ones. A tag that can't make its object ({ data } that isn't base64, a { cookie } without a required key) rejects with native_error.

items.title: Returns
items.text:
Promise<unknown>

The result: primitives, strings, and collections of them; on iOS also the structs as objects, an NSURL as a string, an NSDate as seconds, NSData as base64, a UIImage as a base64 PNG and an NSHTTPCookie as its properties (Expires in seconds). Any other object is null.

items.title: Example
items.text:
await ref.current?.call('webView.clearCache', [true]); // Android
await ref.current?.call('scrollView.setContentOffset:animated:', [{ x: 0, y: 100 }, true]); // iOS

items.title: evaluate()
items.text:
evaluate(script): Promise<unknown>

Runs an expression (not statements) in the page's main frame and awaits it.

Resolves with its value through JSON: null for what JSON can't encode (a function, NaN, a cycle), a Date as its ISO string. The value is the page's, so treat it as page data. Rejects with a CodedError: script_error, navigated or unavailable. There is no timeout: a page can hold a call until it navigates. On Android with a WebView older than 83 it rejects with unavailable.

items.title: get()
items.text:
get(key): Promise<unknown>

Reads a platform setting, root.key, and resolves with its value through JSON, as call converts results.

The roots and keys are those of IOSSettings and AndroidSettings.

It reads the WebView as it is when the call arrives: a navigation doesn't reject it. Rejects with a CodedError: not_found, unavailable (Android) or native_error.

items.title: Example
items.text:
const bounces = await ref.current?.get('scrollView.bounces'); // iOS
const textZoom = await ref.current?.get('settings.textZoom'); // Android

items.title: goBack()
items.text:
goBack(): void

Goes back one page; does nothing unless canGoBack.

On Android, as Chrome's back button, it also skips the history entries a page added without a user gesture (pushState, a hash change) and the page that added them.

items.title: goForward()
items.text:
goForward(): void

Goes forward one page; does nothing unless canGoForward.

items.title: hook()
items.text:
hook(name, method, args?): Promise<unknown>

Calls the method handler the native hook name registered with context.handle, with args, and resolves with its reply; both cross as JSON.

The reply converts as call's results do. Rejects with a CodedError: not_found or native_error. A navigation or a crash doesn't settle a call whose handler hasn't replied; only an unmount does.

items.title: reload()
items.text:
reload(): void

Reloads the page; after a failed load, retries the failed URL.

Sends a POST source again, and lifts the limit on crash recovery.

items.title: stopLoading()
items.text:
stopLoading(): void

Stops the load: its outcome is cancelled, or on Android finished once the page has arrived.

items.title: WebViewRefObject
items.text:
WebViewRefObject = object

What createWebViewRef() returns: a ref that outlives the WebViews mounted with it.

items.title: getState()
items.text:
getState(): NavigationState

The mounted WebView's navigation state, read synchronously.

items.title: subscribe()
items.text:
subscribe(listener): () => void

Calls listener on every state change, including a WebView mounting or unmounting, and returns the unsubscribe.

A subscriber stays across remounts.

items.title: current
items.text:
readonly current: WebViewRef | null

The mounted WebView's ref, or null while none is mounted.

items.title: WebViewSource
items.text:
WebViewSource = { body?: string; headers?: Record<string, string>; readAccessRoot?: string; uri: string; } | { baseUrl?: string; html: string; }

What the WebView loads: a URL, or an HTML string.

items.title: body?
items.text:
optional body?: string

Makes the request a POST with this form-urlencoded body.

Its Content-Type is application/x-www-form-urlencoded unless iOS headers set one; Android sends no headers. reload() sends the POST again; crash recovery doesn't.

items.title: headers?
items.text:
optional headers?: Record<string, string>

Sent with the first request only, not on later navigations.

items.title: readAccessRoot?
items.text:
optional readAccessRoot?: string

iOS

For a file:// uri, the file:// directory the page may read, which must contain the file. Without it, or when it isn't a file: URL or doesn't contain the file (a warning says so), the file's directory.

items.title: uri
items.text:
uri: string

The URL to load.

A file:// URL reads only within readAccessRoot on iOS; Android needs android.settings.allowFileAccess, which lets a file: page read any file the app can.

items.title: baseUrl?
items.text:
optional baseUrl?: string

The page's URL: its relative URLs resolve against it, and it has this origin. Without it, about:blank.

items.title: defaultNavigationRules
items.text:
defaultNavigationRules: readonly NavigationRule[]

The rules navigationRules has when it is unset: file: is blocked, http(s) loads in place, and any other scheme opens externally from the main frame when a user gesture started it (NavigationRule.userInitiated).

Anything else, a subframe's or one without a gesture, is blocked: a page that launches an app from a script or timer, and on iOS also from a click handler or from a redirect after a form POST (an OAuth myapp://callback).

Frozen; spread it after your own rules to keep it.

items.title: reactNativeWebViewMessages
items.text:
reactNativeWebViewMessages: InjectedScript

react-native-webview's messaging, for injectedScripts, carried by the bridge event rnw.

The page's window.ReactNativeWebView.postMessage(data) arrives as String(data), and what you emit reaches the page as a message event on window on iOS and on document on Android, as react-native-webview does.

It needs the bridge prop: only the main frame of the pages in allowedOrigins gets window.ReactNativeWebView, and only postMessage: there is no injectedObjectJson. Its origins are ['*'], since the bridge already scopes it.

items.title: Example
items.text:
const bridge = createBridge({ allowedOrigins: ['https://example.com'] });
bridge.on('rnw', (data) => console.log(data)); // the page called ReactNativeWebView.postMessage(data)
bridge.emit('rnw', 'hello'); // the page gets a message event whose data is 'hello'

<WebView source={{ uri: 'https://example.com' }} bridge={bridge} injectedScripts={[reactNativeWebViewMessages]} />;
